extracted.intended_audience: law students, environmental lawyers, regulators, policymakers, NGOs, and informed public interested in U.S. GHG regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes U.S. regulatory standards, statutory interpretations, permit programs, and scientific bases relevant to regulating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions under the Clean Air Act (CAA). Useful for understanding legal tests, applicability rules, and regulatory mechanisms used by EPA and states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment finding under CAA section 202(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrator found that six greenhouse gases in the atmosphere – CO2, CH4, N2O, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, and sulfur hexafluoride – may reasonably be anticipated to endanger both public health and public welfare; and that GHG emissions from mobile sources covered under CAA section 202(a) contribute to the total greenhouse gas air pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Administrator relied primarily upon assessment reports and other scientific documents produced by the IPCC, the U.S. Global Change Research Program, and the National Research Council in reaching the conclusions underlying the endangerment finding. The finding is a prerequisite for establishing regulations for GHGs from mobile sources under CAA §202(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific evidentiary standard for regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses comprehensive, advanced, and thoroughly reviewed scientific assessment reports (e.g., IPCC, USGCRP, NRC) as the primary basis for major regulatory determinations about GHGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory findings (like the endangerment finding) are grounded in these bodies of work; agencies rely on peer-reviewed assessments as the most authoritative summary of climate science when making statutory determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPCC definition of 'climate change'
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change is 'a change in the state of the climate that can be identified (e.g. using statistical tests) by changes in the mean and/or the variability of its properties, and that persists for an extended period, typically decades or longer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition covers any change over time, whether due to natural variability or human activity, and underpins how regulators characterize long-term climatic trends and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHG physical properties relevant to regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Greenhouse gases retain heat in the atmosphere, accumulate when emitted faster than removed, influence Earth's energy balance for decades to centuries, and become well mixed globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties (long atmospheric lifetime, global mixing) are used to justify treating GHGs as global pollutants and inform regulatory scope and timing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health endangerment categories
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA identified categories by which GHGs could reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health: direct temperature effects (e.g., heat-related deaths), effects on air quality (ozone formation exacerbating respiratory illnesses), effects on extreme weather events, and effects on climate-sensitive diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific pathways are cited as mechanistic bases for concluding that GHGs threaten public health, and thus support statutory endangerment findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public welfare endangerment categories
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA identified categories by which GHGs could reasonably be anticipated to endanger public welfare: agriculture (crop failure risk), forestry (wildfires, insect outbreaks), water resources (shrinking snowpack affecting supplies), sea level rise (exacerbating storm-surge flooding), energy (increased peak demand and infrastructure vulnerability), ecosystems and wildlife, ocean warming and acidification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These welfare impacts provide the statutory basis (public welfare) for regulatory action and help justify the nationwide scope of GHG regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDV Rule applicability and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Light‑Duty Vehicle (LDV) Rule applies to light‑duty vehicles, light‑duty trucks, and medium‑duty passenger vehicles for model years 2012–2016 and establishes CO2 standards (gram/mile) per manufacturer's fleet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance is determined by calculating a production‑weighted fleet average emissions rate at the end of a model year and comparing it to the applicable fleet average emission standard; standards become more stringent year-to-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDV Rule ancillary pollutant standards (N2O, CH4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The LDV Rule includes standards of 0.010 gram/mile for N2O and 0.030 gram/mile for CH4 as anti‑backsliding measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These low-level standards address additional GHGs already emitted from motor vehicles and prevent regression in performance for those species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory flexibility via banking and trading credits
rubrics_metrics.description: LDV Rule allows manufacturers to bank emissions credits when fleet average CO2 emissions are less than the standard, then use credits where models fall short or sell credits to other manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banking and trading are intended to address technological feasibility, lead time, and cost of compliance and to promote environmental objectives while providing flexibility to regulated entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: State preemption under CAA §209(a) and waiver under §209(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: §209(a) prohibits states from adopting standards for emissions from new motor vehicles; §209(b) allows EPA to waive this prohibition for states that had adopted standards prior to March 30, 1966 (California) if the state demonstrates standards are at least as protective of public health as federal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: California is the only state eligible for waivers under §209(b); once EPA grants a waiver for particular standards, other states may generally adopt California's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSR program structure (PSD and NNSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: New Source Review (NSR) comprises Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) for areas meeting NAAQS and for pollutants without NAAQS, and Nonattainment NSR (NNSR) for areas not meeting NAAQS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSD permits require use of Best Available Control Technology (BACT) and air quality modeling demonstrating the source will not cause or contribute to NAAQS violations; permits issued by EPA or authorized state/local agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and timing of 'regulated NSR pollutant'
rubrics_metrics.description: A pollutant becomes a 'regulated NSR pollutant' when a provision of the Act or regulations requires actual control of that pollutant, not when regulations merely require monitoring or reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA clarified that the pollutant is treated as regulated for NSR purposes when the control requirements take effect (not merely upon promulgation), affecting when PSD obligations apply to GHGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT selection process and considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: BACT is established through a five‑step analytical process resulting in selection of one or more methods to reduce emissions and setting emission limits and operational restrictions, applied case‑by‑case considering site‑ and source‑specific factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities may temper the stringency of the final emission limit for compelling adverse economic, energy, or environmental considerations; BACT thus blends command‑and‑control with site‑sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability thresholds and the Tailoring Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Because typical PSD thresholds (100/250 tpy) would have brought tens of thousands more sources under PSD if GHGs were included, EPA's Tailoring Rule raised the major source regulatory threshold for GHGs to 100,000 tons per year CO2‑equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailoring Rule was adopted to avoid 'absurd results' and unbearable administrative burdens; threshold adjustments were an agency response to statutory structure and practicability concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court limitation on PSD/Title V GHG regulation (anyway sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court (5‑4) remanded the Tailoring Rule, holding EPA could only require 'anyway' sources—those subject to PSD because of emissions of non‑GHG pollutants—to comply with PSD and Title V requirements for GHGs, excluding the Step 2 sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This judicial limitation constrained the universe of sources subject to GHG permitting under the existing statutory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative burden metrics for PSD permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated average administrative costs for a PSD permit: applicants expend 866 hours and $125,120; permitting authorities expend 301 hours and $23,280.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quantified burdens are used to argue about practicability and the need for tailoring applicability thresholds when expanding PSD to GHGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional PSD focus on large industrial sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically PSD targeted large industrial sources (power plants, refineries, manufacturing) emitting more than 250 tpy (sometimes 100 tpy) of regulated pollutants; inclusion of GHGs risks sweeping in many nontraditional sources (office buildings, malls) because GHG emissions volumes are far greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction informed policy choices (e.g., Tailoring Rule) to limit regulatory reach to major emitters that were the original focus of PSD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of CAA section 111 to regulate EGUs and refineries
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA announced it would establish GHG standards for new and modified electric generating units (EGUs) and petroleum refineries under CAA §111(b) and set emissions guidelines for existing sources under §111(d) through settlement agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timelines (e.g., final standards for EGUs and refineries scheduled in settlement) and the choice of §111 pathways illustrate alternative statutory mechanisms for addressing stationary‑source GHG emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques of prescriptive regulation and EPA responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescriptive regulation is criticized as overly rigid and uneconomical because it may not incentivize emissions reductions beyond minimums nor achieve benefits at lowest cost. EPA's LDV Rule addressed these critiques by phasing increasing stringency and building in flexibilities (banking/trading).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers weigh tradeoffs between command‑and‑control approaches and flexible market mechanisms when designing GHG regulations under existing statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of NGOs, states, and litigation in triggering regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: NGO petitions and litigation (e.g., Massachusetts v. EPA) pressured EPA to act; settlement agreements with NGOs and states can obligate EPA to issue standards under statutory timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder influence and litigation history are practical considerations shaping regulatory outcomes and agency timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: California federal-state program convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: After EPA approval of California's waiver for GHG vehicle standards, California and EPA worked to converge programs allowing automakers to produce a single national fleet complying with both programs; fifteen states adopted California's standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intergovernmental coordination and program convergence are mechanisms to reduce compliance complexity and encourage broader state adoption of stricter standards.
